chunks.heading: Defining academic integrity

shapes.quote: Academic integrity refers to the *values* that underpin not only the scholarly work of such a community, but also the work you complete on your learning journey as you move from the edge to its centre, from being a novice to an expert.

Different universities will have different interpretations of these values, but the International Center for Academic Integrity (ICAI, 2021) has helpfully identified six of what it calls the 'fundamental' values of academic integrity.

pathwayTags.evidence: An example of honesty in practice is the need to reference your sources accurately (more on this below).

shapes.quote: Put simply, referencing refers to the practice of acknowledging where the knowledge you are using in your work comes from.

Yet referencing is about much more than avoiding plagiarism. When looked at in the context of marking criteria, referencing becomes a highly valuable tool which can help you to evidence your competencies against it.

pathwayTags.evidence: The clearest example of where academic integrity meets learning at university is in referencing.

chunks.heading: Referencing styles

shapes.quote: In our experience, the most commonly used referencing styles are (in no particular order): Author-date (usually referred to as 'Harvard' in UK institutions) – used widely across a number of disciplines; MHRA (Modern Humanities Research Association) – mainly used in humanities disciplines; Chicago (Chicago University Press) – again, often used in humanities disciplines; APA (American Psychological Association) – principally, psychology, but also social sciences and some business-related disciplines; Vancouver – for medical/clinical-related disciplines; IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers) – for engineering, computer science, and related disciplines; and OSCOLA (Oxford University Standard for Citation of Legal Authorities) – for law.

pathwayTags.evidence: Much depends on the discipline in which you're studying; but, that said, on some programmes, particularly at postgraduate level, you might be expected to use more than one style.

shapes.quote: When compared to quoting, as described above, paraphrasing is clearly far more skilful.
